The Giant Pacific scallop Patinopecten caurinus exhibits a reproductive strategy shaped by the cold waters of its subarctic habitat. At a sustained temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], field studies measured a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 15% [GSI = 15%]. The measurement was derived from dissections of adult specimens collected during the pre-spawning season in the Gulf of Alaska, where bottom temperatures remain near 9 °C throughout much of the year. Such comparative data underscore the interspecific variation in reproductive allocation among pectinids and provide a baseline for assessing how changing ocean temperatures might alter energy partitioning in these commercially valuable bivalves.

The early life history of Patinopecten caurinus begins with an egg of approximately 200 micrometers in diameter, from which a fertilized ovum emerges. Based on this egg dimension, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], a value representing the mass of the newly released zygote prior to any exogenous feeding. This minute initial size is typical of bivalves that produce large numbers of small, lecithotrophic eggs, and it contrasts with the relatively larger eggs of some direct-developing pectinids. After a brief period of yolk-dependent development, the embryo hatches and the resulting trochophore larva begins its planktonic existence. Measurements of the prodissoconch I stage, which corresponds to the shell formed during the egg and early larval period, indicate a shell length at metamorphosis of 0.06 centimeters  by the time the larva achieves metamorphic competence and undergoes settlement.

Growth trajectories for Patinopecten caurinus indicate that individuals can attain a substantial ultimate shell length of 17 centimeters [Li = 17 centimeters] under favorable conditions, making this one of the largest scallops in the northern Pacific. This asymptotic size is typically reached after several years of steady somatic expansion, with shell accretion rates slowing considerably once the animal approaches its maximum dimension. Measurements from dredge surveys in the Bering Sea and along the continental shelf of British Columbia consistently record adult specimens within a range of 14 to 17 centimeters, with the upper bound confirmed by the largest individuals observed in long-term monitoring programs. The shell itself is robust, characterized by broad radial ribs and a deep byssal notch, and it supports the scallop's epibenthic lifestyle on soft sediments. This ultimate shell length is a key life history parameter that influences predator avoidance, filtration capacity, and reproductive output.

Longevity in this species is considerable, with maximum lifespan documented at 21 years [am = 21 years] when individuals are maintained at a constant temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to over 7,600 days, places Patinopecten caurinus among the longer-lived pectinids and is consistent with the slow growth and late maturation typical of many cold-water bivalves. Age determinations are typically made from annual growth increments visible in the shell's hinge plate, with validation provided by mark-recapture studies and bomb radiocarbon dating. The species' ability to persist for two decades or more reflects a life history strategy that prioritizes somatic durability and repeated reproductive events over rapid turnover. In terms of developmental timing, sexual maturation is attained after a prolonged juvenile phase; puberty is reached approximately 3 years since birth [tp = approximately 3 years since birth], specifically at 1,095 days post-hatching and at the same ambient temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C].

The extended juvenile period prior to the attainment of puberty has implications for population dynamics, as recruitment into the reproductive cohort requires a multi-year investment in somatic growth. The wet weight at birth of 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams] results from an egg diameter of roughly 200 micrometers, a size that supplies sufficient yolk reserves for the lecithotrophic larva to reach the shell length at metamorphosis of 0.06 centimeters  before it must begin filter-feeding on phytoplankton. This initial mass is two to three orders of magnitude lower than that reported for some direct-developing bivalves, reinforcing the trade-off between offspring size and fecundity observed across marine invertebrates. The gonadosomatic index of 15% [GSI = 15%] was recorded at 9 °C [T = 9 °C]. Taken together, these life history parameters—from the microscopic egg to the 17-centimeter ultimate shell length (17 centimeters) [Li = 17 centimeters] and the 21-year lifespan (21 years) [am = 21 years]—paint a portrait of a slow-paced, long-lived pectinid finely tuned to its subarctic environment at a temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C].
